title: 403(b) retirement plan investments (H.R. 1013)
headline: Changes federal securities laws so 403(b) retirement plans, used by many teachers, nonprofit and hospital workers, can offer collective investment trusts and insurance-company separate accounts, as 401(k) plans already can. The House passed it on November 11, 2026; it now goes to the Senate.

p: This describes the version the House passed, which includes changes recommended by the House Financial Services Committee. The official Congress.gov summary was written for the bill as introduced.

Collective investment trusts are pooled investment funds run by banks or trust companies; insurance-company separate accounts are similar pooled funds run by insurers. Both are often used in 401(k) plans.
The bill extends the exemptions in federal securities laws that 401(k) plans already use for these products, so 403(b) plans could offer them too.

A 2022 retirement law (SECURE 2.0) changed the tax code to let 403(b) plans use these investments, but the matching securities-law changes were never made, so in practice most 403(b) plans still can't offer them.

changes: Allows 403(b) plans to offer collective investment trusts and insurance-company separate accounts without registering them as public securities.
Treats these products in 403(b) plans more like they are already treated in 401(k) plans.
affects: Workers saving in 403(b) plans, including public school teachers and employees of charities, hospitals, universities and churches.
Employers that sponsor 403(b) plans and the banks, insurers and investment firms that manage these funds.

for.point: Teachers, nurses and nonprofit workers should have access to the same lower-cost investment options that private-sector 401(k) savers already have.
The bill fixes a gap left after the 2022 retirement law and would help savers at charities and educational institutions.

against.point: Many 403(b) plans are not covered by the federal pension law (ERISA), so removing securities-law protections leaves those savers with too little federal oversight.
against.who: Reps. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) and Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.)

next: The bill goes to the Senate, where Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.) leads a companion bill. If the Senate does not pass it before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, it would have to be reintroduced.
